Honorable Ministers, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I call to order the 2nd meeting of the 2025 sessions of the Economic and Social Council Forum on Financing for Development follow-up. Excellencies, I invite the Forum to continue its considerations of Agenda Item 2B, thematic panel discussions to hold the 3 consecutive ministerial fireside chats this afternoon. I first invite the forum to turn to Ministerial Fireside Chat 3 on revitalizing development cooperation for impact and inclusion. I'm pleased to invite Her Excellency Istina Renat Hayem Istina Secretary for International Development of Norway to make introductory remarks. Excellency, you have the floor.

Thank you. The development cooperation landscape is going through dramatic changes. We are expecting a steep decline in official development assistance in 2025 from a record level in 2023. The decline is likely to continue. At the same time, ODA is expected to address an increasing number of challenges. Norway has for 2 consecutive years provided more than 1% of gross national income as ODA, well above the UN target of 0.7%. We will remain a consistent, reliable development partner, and we strongly encourage all countries to contribute to international development according to their capacity, including emerging economies. The Financing for Sustainable Development Report 2024 describes an ongoing fragmentation The average grant is only half the size of 20 years ago, while the number of bilateral and multilateral donor agencies has tripled. We have been discussing reforms of development cooperation architecture and the multilateral system for some time now. This will now happen, probably faster and more drastic than most of us would have preferred. Now we should seize the opportunity to address the effectiveness and fragmentation of development cooperation as a part of the FFD4 process. The downward trend in ODA presents a critical opportunity to use ODA more strategically. It should be a tool for development countries to raise domestic revenues. To create an enabling environment that attracts sustainable private investments and capital. The multilateral development banks are key providers of development finance and have a unique ability to leverage donor contributions. They are multilateral institutions with the ability to mobilize private capital at scale. The MDBs have taken significant steps to further increase efficiency and effectiveness through updating mandates, cutting project preparation time, and improving crisis preparedness and response. They offer knowledge and evidence-based policy advice and capacity building on public financial management and transparency, debt management, tax policy, climate investments, investment in women and girls, pro-poor spending, and social safety nets. I am pleased to see that this year's FFD Forum has such a strong emphasis on cooperation between the Bretton Woods institutions and the UN system. We must work across all 3 dimensions of sustainability— economic, social, and environmental— Each dimension depends on the others. Climate change undermines past achievements and is a major threat to future development prospects. With limited resources, we should pursue an integrated approach, addressing several goals at the same time, linking the local and the global level. It is becoming more and more difficult to imagine development without taking climate and environmental consideration into account. Furthermore, transparency and accountability are essential pillars of effective development. They ensure that resources are used efficiently and corruption risk is minimized. This allows stakeholders, especially governments, civil society, and citizens, to track financing progress and gaps and hold institutions responsible for results. FFD offers a unique opportunity to set a new course for international development cooperation. I look forward to a fruitful discussion here today. Thank you so much.
